screens.title: Unit Testing with Hardhat
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why Hardhat is a preferred environment for local Ethereum development and how to start writing reliable unit tests for Solidity contracts. We'll orient on the pieces that work together: Hardhat provides a local in-memory network and a developer workflow, Mocha structures tests, Chai expresses assertions, and Waffle-style matchers make Solidity checks readable. You will see a concrete startup path — initialize a project, install the testing plugins and ethers, create a simple contract, and write tests that deploy fresh instances in a beforeEach hook. Along the way we'll point out common beginner mistakes like forgetting to await transactions or reusing a contract instance across tests. This matters because tests are developers’ safety net: they verify behavior, prevent regressions, and make refactors safe. By the end you'll be able to run npx hardhat test, interpret the output, and fix failing assertions with confidence. One key idea to hold on to is test isolation: each it block should run from a known state so a bug in one test can't hide another. Ready to set up your first project and write your first passing test?

screens.title: What you'll be able to do
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on practical skills you will use immediately when testing Solidity contracts with Hardhat. First, you'll set up and configure a new Hardhat project so your environment compiles, deploys, and tests contracts locally. Second, you'll understand the structure of a test file written with Mocha and Chai, including describe blocks, it test cases, and asynchronous behavior. Third, you'll install and use testing helpers such as the Hardhat Chai matchers and ethers to write expressive assertions against events, reverts, and contract state. Finally, you'll learn to deploy fresh contract instances in test hooks so each test runs from a known state. Each objective maps to a small verified milestone you can check after completing the hands-on activity. screens.title: Applied testing skills
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on applying your tests in practice. You will run tests with npx hardhat test, interpret the console output to determine which assertions failed, and use failing tests as guides for debugging. You will also learn to avoid common errors: missing awaits, reusing a deployed instance across tests, and exposing private keys in test scripts. Finally, you'll author at least three unit tests for a Counter contract as practice — checking initial state, increment, and decrement behavior — and optionally test a getter. Practicing these operations helps you build confidence: running tests frequently catches regressions early, and intentionally creating a failing assertion lets you observe how Hardhat reports problems. After this you should be comfortable reading stack traces, verifying transaction receipts when necessary, and ensuring test isolation with beforeEach. A short reflection: when you next write a test, ask whether the test would still pass if run alone and whether any global state could silently change the outcome.

screens.title: What is Hardhat and the testing stack?
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat is a development environment that gives you a fast, in-memory blockchain and a plugin ecosystem so you can compile, deploy, and test Solidity contracts locally. Think of it as a sandboxed Ethereum node that resets cleanly for every test run. Mocha is the JavaScript test runner Hardhat uses to structure tests using describe and it blocks. Chai is the assertion library that gives us expressive statements like expect(value). to. equal(100). Waffle-style matchers, available through the Hardhat Chai matchers plugin, extend Chai with Solidity-aware assertions for events and reverts. ethers. js is the library used to get a ContractFactory, deploy contracts, and call or transact with them in tests. A concrete example: in a test you call ethers. getContractFactory to create a deployment abstraction and then call deploy(100) to pass a constructor parameter. A common misconception is to treat these pieces as interchangeable — they are complementary. Hardhat provides the environment and task runner, Mocha organizes test logic, Chai describes expectations, and ethers talks to contracts. Why this matters: using the stack together lets you write isolated, readable tests that deploy fresh contract instances, assert on state and events, and fail loudly when behavior changes. When you next write a test, check that your assertions are clear, and that the testing stack you pick supports the Solidity patterns you need.

keyIdea.title: Testing stack roles
keyIdea.text: Hardhat provides the runtime and network; Mocha structures tests; Chai and Waffle express assertions; ethers performs deployments and calls.

content.html:
Core Concept

What is Hardhat and the testing stack?

Understand the role of Hardhat, Mocha, Chai, Waffle matchers, and ethers in unit testing.

Definitions
  • Hardhat: Local Ethereum network and toolchain for compiling, running scripts, and testing.
  • Mocha: Test runner providing describe and it structure.
  • Chai: Assertion library used with expect style for readable checks.
  • ethers.js: Library to deploy and interact with contracts in tests.
Example
Use ethers.getContractFactory and call deploy(100) to construct a SimpleStorage with an initial value in a beforeEach hook.
Why this composition matters

Combined, these tools let you create reproducible test environments, deploy fresh contract instances for isolation, and write clear assertions about behavior and events.

Common misconception: "My tests can share one deployed contract across many it blocks." That often hides stateful interactions and causes flakiness; prefer beforeEach for isolation.

Key Takeaway

Treat the stack as roles: environment, structure, assertions, and RPC layer; use each for its purpose to write robust tests.

screens.title: Initialize a new Hardhat project
screens.narratorSegment: Starting a Hardhat project is a short set of commands that prepares a testable workspace. First ensure you have Node. js and npm installed. Then create a directory, run npm init -y to initialize a package file, and install Hardhat as a dev dependency using npm install --save-dev hardhat. The next command is npx hardhat, which launches an interactive setup. Choose the JavaScript project option unless you prefer TypeScript. This scaffolds hardhat. config. js, a contracts directory, a scripts directory, and a test directory. Why these steps matter: hardhat. config. js sets the compiler version and plugin configuration used during tests; the test directory is where Mocha looks for test files by default. A concrete example: mkdir my-hardhat-project; cd my-hardhat-project; npm init -y; npm install --save-dev hardhat; npx hardhat. A common pitfall is running npx hardhat without installing hardhat locally; the interactive prompt may still run but installing as a dev dependency ensures repeatable CI runs. Another mistake is committing local node_modules or leaking private keys in the config — keep secrets out of your repository. After scaffolding run npx hardhat test to confirm the example tests pass. As you practice, notice how a fresh project gives you a predictable starting point for writing clean, isolated tests.

keyIdea.title: Scaffold reproducibly
keyIdea.text: Scaffolding with npx hardhat creates the standard folders and config so tests run consistently across machines and CI.

content.html:
Process Flow

Initialize a new Hardhat project

Run a short sequence of commands to scaffold a project prepared for testing.

Step-by-step
  1. mkdir my-hardhat-project and cd into it.
  2. npm init -y to create package.json.
  3. npm install --save-dev hardhat to add Hardhat locally.
  4. npx hardhat and choose "Create a JavaScript project" to scaffold files.
Quick command
mkdir my-hardhat-project
cd my-hardhat-project
npm init -y
npm install --save-dev hardhat
npx hardhat
Notes & pitfalls

If you skip local installation you may depend on a global version; keep Hardhat in devDependencies for reproducibility.

Misconception: "Scaffolding is optional." Without a standard scaffold you'll have to configure Mocha, directories, and compiler options manually, which increases friction.

Why it matters

A stable scaffold reduces setup errors and makes tests portable across collaborators and CI systems.

screens.title: Install testing helpers and ethers
screens.narratorSegment: To write expressive Solidity tests you'll commonly install two groups of helpers: the Hardhat Chai matchers and ethers. The matchers package exposes Waffle-style assertions for Solidity such as expect(tx). to. emit(contract, 'Event') and expect(fn). to. be. revertedWith. Install them with npm install --save-dev @nomicfoundation/hardhat-chai-matchers @nomiclabs/hardhat-ethers ethers. The @nomiclabs plugin integrates ethers. js into Hardhat, so your tests can use ethers. getContractFactory and other convenience helpers. After installing, update hardhat. config. js to include the matchers plugin if necessary or import it within a test helper. A concrete example: after installation you can write expect(await simpleStorage. get()). to. equal(100) or expect(myTx). to. emit(simpleStorage, 'ValueSet'). A common misunderstanding is to rely only on generic Chai assertions; while those work for basic checks, the Solidity matchers provide clearer semantics for events and reverts that would otherwise require manual log decoding. Why this matters in practice: these plugins reduce boilerplate when testing contract-specific behavior and make failure messages easier to read. When you set up a new project, install these helper libraries immediately so your first tests are expressive and maintainable. Install testing helpers and ethers means add @nomicfoundation/hardhat-chai-matchers and ethers so your tests can deploy contracts and assert solidity behaviors clearly.. In practical terms, make assertions readable and deployable with plugins. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

Install testing helpers and ethers

Add Chai matchers and ethers to make tests expressive and able to deploy contracts.

Install these packages
npm install --save-dev @nomicfoundation/hardhat-chai-matchers @nomiclabs/hardhat-ethers ethers

These packages give you Solidity-aware assertions and the ability to deploy and interact with contracts through ethers.js.

Example assertion
expect(await simpleStorage.get()).to.equal(100)
Why the matchers help
  • They provide event and revert checks tailored for Solidity.
  • They produce clearer failure messages than generic assertions for contract interactions.
  • They reduce manual decoding or receipt checks in many common cases.
Key Takeaway

Install testing plugins early so your assertions are idiomatic and maintainable.

screens.title: SimpleStorage.sol — a minimal contract to test
screens.narratorSegment: SimpleStorage is a deliberately minimal Solidity contract used to teach testing fundamentals. It exposes a public uint called storedData, a constructor that sets an initial value, a setter function set(uint256) and a getter get() that returns the stored value. This small surface area is ideal for unit tests because each function has predictable, verifiable behavior. A concrete example: deploying SimpleStorage with constructor parameter 100 means expect(await simpleStorage. get()). to. equal(100) should pass. When writing tests, treat public variables and view functions as simple read assertions, and treat transactions like set calls as state-changing actions you must await. A common misunderstanding is to expect set to return its new value; instead set is a transaction and you should wait for transaction confirmation, then call get to assert state. Another subtle point: marking storedData public creates an automatic getter in Solidity, but tests often prefer an explicit get function for clarity. Why this matters: small, focused contracts let you practice test isolation, assertions, and proper use of await before moving to more complex contracts. Try to write tests that assert a constructor-initialized state, then call set and assert the updated state, and finally chain multiple updates to confirm state transitions behave as expected.

keyIdea.title: Small contract, big lessons
keyIdea.text: SimpleStorage demonstrates constructor initialization, state changes via transactions, and the need to await calls before asserting state.

content.html:
Definition

SimpleStorage.sol — a minimal contract to test

A compact contract that illustrates constructor initialization, state changes, and getters.

Contract (visual)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract SimpleStorage {
    uint256 public storedData;

    constructor(uint256 initialData) {
        storedData = initialData;
    }

    function set(uint256 x) public {
        storedData = x;
    }

    function get() public view returns (uint256) {
        return storedData;
    }
}
Testing implications
  • Constructor arguments determine initial assertions in your first test.
  • set is a transaction: await it, then call the getter to assert updated state.
  • get is a view that returns a promise you must await in tests.
Example assertion
expect(await simpleStorage.get()).to.equal(100)
Common mistake

Forgetting to await a transaction or a call can return a pending promise and cause false test behavior.

screens.title: Write your first test file
screens.narratorSegment: A typical test file in Hardhat uses Mocha's describe and it blocks, along with hooks like beforeEach to deploy a clean contract instance for each test. Start by importing expect from Chai and ethers from Hardhat. In a describe block name the contract under test, then use beforeEach to get the ContractFactory and deploy a new instance with the constructor argument you want. Each it block describes a specific behavior and contains assertions that use await to resolve promises. For example, in the first it test you might assert expect(await simpleStorage. get()). to. equal(100). For state changes, call await simpleStorage. set(newValue) and then await the getter to assert the updated value. A concrete test pattern looks like: beforeEach deploy with 100, it asserts initial value, another it awaits a set to 200 and asserts the new value. A common misconception is thinking transaction-returning functions return the new state — they don't; you must await the transaction and then read the state. Also avoid reusing a contract deployed in one it block for another. Why this structure matters: it keeps tests independent and easy to debug. When a test fails, the failing it description and assertion message guide you to the problematic behavior so you can fix either the test or the contract logic.

keyIdea.title: Test structure pattern
keyIdea.text: Use describe to group tests, beforeEach to redeploy fresh contracts, and it blocks with await and expect assertions to verify behavior.

content.html:
Process Flow

Write your first test file

A code walkthrough that shows the common deployment and assertion pattern.

Test file (visual)
const { expect } = require("chai");
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

describe("SimpleStorage", function () {
  let SimpleStorage;
  let simpleStorage;

  beforeEach(async function () {
    SimpleStorage = await ethers.getContractFactory("SimpleStorage");
    simpleStorage = await SimpleStorage.deploy(100);
  });

  it("Should deploy with the correct initial value", async function () {
    expect(await simpleStorage.get()).to.equal(100);
  });
});
Explanations & tips
  • beforeEach: Deploy a fresh contract instance before each it block to avoid shared state.
  • await: Await both deployment and subsequent contract calls or transactions.
  • expect: Use expect(...).to.equal(...) for exact checks; use matchers for events or reverts.
Common mistake

Forgetting to await deployment or calls leads to unresolved promises and incorrect assertions.

screens.title: Using beforeEach and test isolation
screens.narratorSegment: Test isolation is the practice of ensuring each test runs from a known, clean starting state. In Hardhat tests you achieve isolation by deploying a new contract instance in a hook like beforeEach. Using beforeEach means every it block gets a fresh SimpleStorage with the constructor value you specify; therefore state changes in one test cannot affect another. A concrete example: if one test calls set(200) and another test expects the initial value 100, both will pass if the contract is redeployed in beforeEach. If you instead deployed once outside of beforeEach and mutated state across tests, subsequent assertions could fail unpredictably. Another subtle point: before is a hook that runs once per describe; use it when expensive setup can be shared and when tests are read-only, but prefer beforeEach for stateful contracts. A common assumption among learners is that tests run in isolation by default; in fact the test file must explicitly redeploy or reset state. Why this matters: isolation makes tests deterministic and makes failing tests easier to diagnose because they only reflect one scenario. Before finishing a test file, ask whether any test depends on the side effects of another; if so, refactor to use beforeEach to deploy fresh instances.

keyIdea.text: Use beforeEach to deploy fresh contract instances so each test starts from the same known state, preventing hidden dependencies between tests.

content.html:
Process Flow

Using beforeEach and test isolation

Deploy fresh instances so tests do not influence one another and remain deterministic.

beforeEach pattern
beforeEach(async function () {
  SimpleStorage = await ethers.getContractFactory("SimpleStorage");
  simpleStorage = await SimpleStorage.deploy(100);
});

This ensures each it gets a fresh SimpleStorage seeded with 100.

Why not reuse a single deployment?
  • Reusing a deployed instance can hide stateful bugs and make tests order-dependent.
  • Isolated tests are easier to parallelize and faster to reason about.
Key Takeaway

Prefer beforeEach for stateful tests. Use before only when setup is expensive and state is read-only.

screens.title: Running tests and interpreting results
screens.narratorSegment: Run your test suite with npx hardhat test. Hardhat will compile contracts and run Mocha tests on its in-memory network, showing passed and failed cases. When a test fails, examine the failing it description and the assertion message. If an assertion compares values, the output usually shows actual and expected values — use that to quickly see where logic diverged. For transaction-related failures, inspect the stack trace and consider printing transaction receipts or event logs. A practical debugging step is to intentionally create a failing assertion to become familiar with Hardhat's error messages. Common beginner errors include forgetting to await a call, which results in unexpected promise values in assertions, or deploying with incorrect constructor arguments. Another common case is expecting a function to return a value on a transaction when it only emits an event or changes state; test authors must read state after the transaction to verify results. Finally, never place mainnet private keys or mnemonics in test scripts — Hardhat provides ephemeral accounts for local tests. After you see a failure, isolate the scenario into a single it block and add console. log statements or use the transaction receipt to inspect intermediate values until you find the discrepancy.

Comparison

Running tests and interpreting results

Run tests and use failure messages and receipts to debug contract behavior.

Command
npx hardhat test

This runs compilation and test execution on Hardhat Network, printing passes and failures with helpful messages.

Debugging checklist
  • Read the failing it description and assertion message for expected vs actual values.
  • Ensure you awaited transactions and calls.
  • Isolate the failing test and add logs or examine the transaction receipt.
  • Check constructor args and deployment timing in beforeEach.
Safety note

Never include real private keys or mnemonics in tests. Use Hardhat's ephemeral accounts for local testing.

screens.title: Activity: Implement tests for Counter.sol
screens.narratorSegment: In this hands-on activity you'll practice the patterns you've learned by writing tests for a Counter contract. The contract exposes a public count, a constructor that sets an initial count, increment and decrement functions, and a getCount view. Create a test file test/Counter. js and import expect and ethers. In beforeEach deploy Counter with a specific initial value, for example 5. Then write three tests: one that asserts the constructor set the initial value using expect(await counter. getCount()). to. equal(initialValue), one that calls await counter. increment() and then asserts the value increased by one, and one that calls await counter. decrement() and then asserts the value decreased by one. Optionally add a test for getCount after multiple operations. As you write tests, watch for missing awaits and ensure beforeEach redeploys the contract so tests remain independent. A practical debugging practice is to intentionally assert the wrong expected value to observe the failure message, then fix the test or contract. This active feedback loop trains you to interpret Hardhat's output quickly. After running npx hardhat test and confirming passing assertions, reflect on how beforeEach, await, and expressive assertions work together to produce reliable tests.

keyIdea.title: Practice builds confidence
keyIdea.text: Implementing tests for Counter.sol reinforces deployment, awaiting transactions, and asserting state changes in a controlled exercise.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Activity: Implement tests for Counter.sol

Write tests that verify constructor initialization, increment, and decrement behavior.

Starter test template
const { expect } = require("chai");
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

describe("Counter", function () {
  let Counter;
  let counter;
  const initialValue = 5;

  beforeEach(async function () {
    Counter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Counter");
    counter = await Counter.deploy(initialValue);
  });

  it("Should deploy with the correct initial count", async function () {
    expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(initialValue);
  });
});
Activity checklist
  • Deploy with a known initial value in beforeEach.
  • Write tests for increment and decrement that await transactions and assert the resulting state.
  • Run npx hardhat test and fix any await or setup errors that appear.
Key Takeaway

Small, repeatable tests build a foundation for testing more complex contract logic later.

What to Remember

Key Concepts — Quick Reference

Await everything
Always await deployments, calls, and transactions before asserting state.
Use beforeEach
Deploy fresh contract instances to keep tests deterministic.
Use matchers
Hardhat Chai matchers simplify event and revert assertions for Solidity behaviors.

Practice by writing a small failing test, read the output, and fix it. That loop teaches you how to interpret test results quickly.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why Hardhat is a preferred environment for local Ethereum development and how to start writing reliable unit tests for Solidity contracts. We'll orient on the pieces that work together: Hardhat provides a local in-memory network and a developer workflow, Mocha structures tests, Chai expresses assertions, and Waffle-style matchers make Solidity checks readable. You will see a concrete startup path — initialize a project, install the testing plugins and ethers, create a simple contract, and write tests that deploy fresh instances in a beforeEach hook. Along the way we'll point out common beginner mistakes like forgetting to await transactions or reusing a contract instance across tests. This matters because tests are developers’ safety net: they verify behavior, prevent regressions, and make refactors safe. By the end you'll be able to run npx hardhat test, interpret the output, and fix failing assertions with confidence. One key idea to hold on to is test isolation: each it block should run from a known state so a bug in one test can't hide another. Ready to set up your first project and write your first passing test?

These objectives focus on practical skills you will use immediately when testing Solidity contracts with Hardhat. First, you'll set up and configure a new Hardhat project so your environment compiles, deploys, and tests contracts locally. Second, you'll understand the structure of a test file written with Mocha and Chai, including describe blocks, it test cases, and asynchronous behavior. Third, you'll install and use testing helpers such as the Hardhat Chai matchers and ethers to write expressive assertions against events, reverts, and contract state. Finally, you'll learn to deploy fresh contract instances in test hooks so each test runs from a known state. Each objective maps to a small verified milestone you can check after completing the hands-on activity. What you'll be able to do means these skills build a repeatable testing workflow: initialize, write, assert, and isolate tests so your contracts behave as expected.. In practical terms, skills and milestones for hardhat testing. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

These objectives focus on applying your tests in practice. You will run tests with npx hardhat test, interpret the console output to determine which assertions failed, and use failing tests as guides for debugging. You will also learn to avoid common errors: missing awaits, reusing a deployed instance across tests, and exposing private keys in test scripts. Finally, you'll author at least three unit tests for a Counter contract as practice — checking initial state, increment, and decrement behavior — and optionally test a getter. Practicing these operations helps you build confidence: running tests frequently catches regressions early, and intentionally creating a failing assertion lets you observe how Hardhat reports problems. After this you should be comfortable reading stack traces, verifying transaction receipts when necessary, and ensuring test isolation with beforeEach. A short reflection: when you next write a test, ask whether the test would still pass if run alone and whether any global state could silently change the outcome.

Hardhat is a development environment that gives you a fast, in-memory blockchain and a plugin ecosystem so you can compile, deploy, and test Solidity contracts locally. Think of it as a sandboxed Ethereum node that resets cleanly for every test run. Mocha is the JavaScript test runner Hardhat uses to structure tests using describe and it blocks. Chai is the assertion library that gives us expressive statements like expect(value). to. equal(100). Waffle-style matchers, available through the Hardhat Chai matchers plugin, extend Chai with Solidity-aware assertions for events and reverts. ethers. js is the library used to get a ContractFactory, deploy contracts, and call or transact with them in tests. A concrete example: in a test you call ethers. getContractFactory to create a deployment abstraction and then call deploy(100) to pass a constructor parameter. A common misconception is to treat these pieces as interchangeable — they are complementary. Hardhat provides the environment and task runner, Mocha organizes test logic, Chai describes expectations, and ethers talks to contracts. Why this matters: using the stack together lets you write isolated, readable tests that deploy fresh contract instances, assert on state and events, and fail loudly when behavior changes. When you next write a test, check that your assertions are clear, and that the testing stack you pick supports the Solidity patterns you need.

Starting a Hardhat project is a short set of commands that prepares a testable workspace. First ensure you have Node. js and npm installed. Then create a directory, run npm init -y to initialize a package file, and install Hardhat as a dev dependency using npm install --save-dev hardhat. The next command is npx hardhat, which launches an interactive setup. Choose the JavaScript project option unless you prefer TypeScript. This scaffolds hardhat. config. js, a contracts directory, a scripts directory, and a test directory. Why these steps matter: hardhat. config. js sets the compiler version and plugin configuration used during tests; the test directory is where Mocha looks for test files by default. A concrete example: mkdir my-hardhat-project; cd my-hardhat-project; npm init -y; npm install --save-dev hardhat; npx hardhat. A common pitfall is running npx hardhat without installing hardhat locally; the interactive prompt may still run but installing as a dev dependency ensures repeatable CI runs. Another mistake is committing local node_modules or leaking private keys in the config — keep secrets out of your repository. After scaffolding run npx hardhat test to confirm the example tests pass. As you practice, notice how a fresh project gives you a predictable starting point for writing clean, isolated tests.

To write expressive Solidity tests you'll commonly install two groups of helpers: the Hardhat Chai matchers and ethers. The matchers package exposes Waffle-style assertions for Solidity such as expect(tx). to. emit(contract, 'Event') and expect(fn). to. be. revertedWith. Install them with npm install --save-dev @nomicfoundation/hardhat-chai-matchers @nomiclabs/hardhat-ethers ethers. The @nomiclabs plugin integrates ethers. js into Hardhat, so your tests can use ethers. getContractFactory and other convenience helpers. After installing, update hardhat. config. js to include the matchers plugin if necessary or import it within a test helper. A concrete example: after installation you can write expect(await simpleStorage. get()). to. equal(100) or expect(myTx). to. emit(simpleStorage, 'ValueSet'). A common misunderstanding is to rely only on generic Chai assertions; while those work for basic checks, the Solidity matchers provide clearer semantics for events and reverts that would otherwise require manual log decoding. Why this matters in practice: these plugins reduce boilerplate when testing contract-specific behavior and make failure messages easier to read. When you set up a new project, install these helper libraries immediately so your first tests are expressive and maintainable. Install testing helpers and ethers means add @nomicfoundation/hardhat-chai-matchers and ethers so your tests can deploy contracts and assert solidity behaviors clearly.. In practical terms, make assertions readable and deployable with plugins. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SimpleStorage is a deliberately minimal Solidity contract used to teach testing fundamentals. It exposes a public uint called storedData, a constructor that sets an initial value, a setter function set(uint256) and a getter get() that returns the stored value. This small surface area is ideal for unit tests because each function has predictable, verifiable behavior. A concrete example: deploying SimpleStorage with constructor parameter 100 means expect(await simpleStorage. get()). to. equal(100) should pass. When writing tests, treat public variables and view functions as simple read assertions, and treat transactions like set calls as state-changing actions you must await. A common misunderstanding is to expect set to return its new value; instead set is a transaction and you should wait for transaction confirmation, then call get to assert state. Another subtle point: marking storedData public creates an automatic getter in Solidity, but tests often prefer an explicit get function for clarity. Why this matters: small, focused contracts let you practice test isolation, assertions, and proper use of await before moving to more complex contracts. Try to write tests that assert a constructor-initialized state, then call set and assert the updated state, and finally chain multiple updates to confirm state transitions behave as expected.

A typical test file in Hardhat uses Mocha's describe and it blocks, along with hooks like beforeEach to deploy a clean contract instance for each test. Start by importing expect from Chai and ethers from Hardhat. In a describe block name the contract under test, then use beforeEach to get the ContractFactory and deploy a new instance with the constructor argument you want. Each it block describes a specific behavior and contains assertions that use await to resolve promises. For example, in the first it test you might assert expect(await simpleStorage. get()). to. equal(100). For state changes, call await simpleStorage. set(newValue) and then await the getter to assert the updated value. A concrete test pattern looks like: beforeEach deploy with 100, it asserts initial value, another it awaits a set to 200 and asserts the new value. A common misconception is thinking transaction-returning functions return the new state — they don't; you must await the transaction and then read the state. Also avoid reusing a contract deployed in one it block for another. Why this structure matters: it keeps tests independent and easy to debug. When a test fails, the failing it description and assertion message guide you to the problematic behavior so you can fix either the test or the contract logic.

Test isolation is the practice of ensuring each test runs from a known, clean starting state. In Hardhat tests you achieve isolation by deploying a new contract instance in a hook like beforeEach. Using beforeEach means every it block gets a fresh SimpleStorage with the constructor value you specify; therefore state changes in one test cannot affect another. A concrete example: if one test calls set(200) and another test expects the initial value 100, both will pass if the contract is redeployed in beforeEach. If you instead deployed once outside of beforeEach and mutated state across tests, subsequent assertions could fail unpredictably. Another subtle point: before is a hook that runs once per describe; use it when expensive setup can be shared and when tests are read-only, but prefer beforeEach for stateful contracts. A common assumption among learners is that tests run in isolation by default; in fact the test file must explicitly redeploy or reset state. Why this matters: isolation makes tests deterministic and makes failing tests easier to diagnose because they only reflect one scenario. Before finishing a test file, ask whether any test depends on the side effects of another; if so, refactor to use beforeEach to deploy fresh instances.

Run your test suite with npx hardhat test. Hardhat will compile contracts and run Mocha tests on its in-memory network, showing passed and failed cases. When a test fails, examine the failing it description and the assertion message. Finally, never place mainnet private keys or mnemonics in test scripts — Hardhat provides ephemeral accounts for local tests. After you see a failure, isolate the scenario into a single it block and add console. log statements or use the transaction receipt to inspect intermediate values until you find the discrepancy.

Let's summarize the key concepts you should remember from this chapter. First, Hardhat is the local network and toolchain that composes with Mocha, Chai and ethers to provide a complete testing workflow. Second, structure your tests using describe and it blocks, deploy fresh contract instances in beforeEach for isolation, and always await transactions and calls so assertions verify resolved values. Third, install and use the Hardhat Chai matchers and ethers to write expressive Solidity-aware assertions for events, state changes, and reverts. Second, redeploy contracts in beforeEach to guarantee test isolation and prevent order-dependent failures. Third, use Hardhat Chai matchers together with ethers to write clear, Solidity-aware assertions for events, reverts, and state.
